Behind the work

My artwork is a digital collage inspired by the Black Arts Movement and by my understanding that Black art can be more than something beautiful; it can also be a way of resisting oppression, preserving memory, building community, and giving Black people the power to define themselves. I began by exploring different visual references on Pinterest and then used Photoshop to layer, arrange, recolor, and combine different images and ideas into one composition that expressed my own interpretation of the movement. I intentionally made the artwork crowded and layered because I did not want Black identity to be represented by one person, one country, one historical moment, or one form of resistance. At the center is a Black woman surrounded by musicians, artists, raised fists, crowds, migration imagery, African patterns, and urban spaces, showing how individual identity can be connected to a much larger history and community. This reflects what I learned about the Black Arts Movement as the “aesthetic and spiritual sister” of Black Power, where art became not simply individual expression but a collective force for political liberation, cultural pride, and community empowerment. The words “Our People, Our Stories, Our Art, Our Power” became the heart of my collage because I see each phrase building on the one before it: people have experiences, those experiences become stories, those stories become art, and having the freedom to create and control that art becomes a form of power. This connects to the Black Arts Movement’s emphasis on creating art for, about, and by Black people while rejecting Eurocentric standards and stereotypical representations of Black life. I also placed the raised fist beside the words “Resist, Create, Build, Heal, Belong” because this unit expanded my understanding of resistance. Resistance can mean openly confronting oppression, but it can also mean creating spaces for Black voices, preserving culture, healing communities, celebrating Black beauty, and building places where Black people feel that they belong. That is also why music and musicians appear throughout my collage. Black music has repeatedly carried history, emotion, community, and resistance across generations, and during the Great Migration, Black migrants carried traditions such as blues and jazz into cities like Chicago and New York, helping create new environments for Black cultural expression. As a Ghanaian, I also wanted my own cultural perspective to have a place in the artwork, which is why I incorporated Ghanaian patterns and Adinkra symbolism into the design. Adinkra is an Akan visual tradition from Ghana in which symbols communicate ideas, values, proverbs, history, and lessons about life; therefore, the symbols are not simply decoration—the artwork itself becomes a way of carrying knowledge and cultural memory from one generation to another. This became especially meaningful to me while studying the Black Arts Movement because one of the movement’s central ideas was cultural self-definition. Black artists deliberately drew from Black and African traditions rather than allowing Eurocentric standards to determine what Black art should look like or what was worthy of artistic value. In that sense, including Adinkra in my collage is itself connected to the purpose of the movement: I am using a visual language from my own African heritage to communicate Black identity. I also see Adinkra connecting directly to “Our People, Our Stories, Our Art, Our Power.” If visual symbols can preserve a people’s values, ideas, and stories, then preserving and creating through your own visual language can itself become a form of cultural power. The Ghanaian elements alongside African American images of migration, music, protest, and urban life are not meant to suggest that Ghanaian and African American histories are the same; instead, they allow me to recognize a broader African diasporic connection and show how art, across different Black experiences, can carry memory, protect culture, communicate identity, and become a means of self-definition. Finally, the words “Past, Present, Future” bring the entire collage together. The Black Arts Movement drew from Black history and cultural traditions, confronted the racial and political realities of its own time, and helped shape later forms of Black expression such as hip-hop and contemporary Black protest art. Through this collage, I wanted to show that Black art can remember the past without being trapped in it, resist the present without being defined only by struggle, and imagine a future in which Black people continue to have the power to tell their own stories.

“Black art can be more than something beautiful; it can also be a way of resisting oppression, preserving memory, building community, and giving Black people the power to define themselves.”

Emmanuel Sefah Acheampong
